Background Amino acid supplementation has been shown to potentially reduced exercise-induced muscle soreness. Thus, the purpose of this study was to examine if branched chain amino acid and carbohydrate (BCAACHO) versus carbohydrate-only sports drink (CHO) supplementation attenuated markers of muscle damage while preserving performance markers following 3 days of intense weight training. Methods Healthy resistance-trained males ( n = 30) performed preliminary testing (T1) whereby they: 1) donated a baseline blood draw, 2) performed knee extensor dynamometry to obtain peak quadriceps isometric and isokinetic torque as well as electromyography (EMG) activity at 60°/s and 120°/s, and 3) performed a one repetition maximum (1RM) barbell back squat. The following week participants performed 10 sets x 5 repetitions at 80 % of their 1RM barbell back squat for 3 consecutive days and 48 h following the third lifting bout participants returned for (T2) testing whereby they repeated the T1 battery. Immediately following and 24 h after the three lifting bouts, participants were randomly assigned to consume one of two commercial products in 600 mL of tap water: 1) BCAAs and CHO (3 g/d L-leucine, 1 g/d L-isoleucine and 2 g/d L-valine with 2 g of CHO; n = 15), or 2) 42 g of CHO only ( n = 15). Additionally, venous blood was drawn 24 h following the first and second lifting bouts and 48 h following the third bout to assess serum myoglobin concentrations, and a visual analog scale was utilized prior, during, and after the 3-d protocol to measure subjective perceptions of muscular soreness. Results There were similar decrements in 1RM squat strength and isokinetic peak torque measures in the BCAA-CHO and CHO groups. Serum myoglobin concentrations ( p = 0.027) and perceived muscle soreness ( p < 0.001) increased over the intervention regardless of supplementation. A group*time interaction was observed for monocyte percentages ( p = 0.01) whereby BCAA-CHO supplementation attenuated increases in this variable over the duration of the protocol compared to CHO supplementation. Conclusion BCAA-CHO supplementation did not reduce decrements in lower body strength or improve select markers of muscle damage/soreness compared to CHO supplementation over three consecutive days of intense lower-body training. Keywords Branched chain amino acids Resistance training Muscle damage Immune system MusclePharm issue-copyright-statement © The Author(s) 2016 Background High-intensity resistance exercise elicits muscle damage and this can be linked to diminished performance [ 1 – 4 ]. Indeed, there have been reviews regarding the efficacy of a wide array of nutritional ergogenic aids in optimizing strength and power [ 5 , 6 ]. Specifically, supplemental protein (e.g. whey, casein, soy, and egg) and/or amino acid ingestion enhances post-exercise recovery by increasing skeletal muscle protein synthesis and reducing muscle proteolysis [ 7 – 9 ] while also potentially reducing post-exercise skeletal muscle inflammation and oxidative stress [ 10 ]. Researchers have also examined if amino acid supplementation can mitigate post-exercise muscle damage. Jackman et al. [ 11 ] reported that branched chain amino acid (BCAA) supplementation attenuated perceived muscle soreness in an untrained population, but supplementation did not alter muscle function following unilateral eccentric knee extension exercise. Howatson et al. [ 12 ] also reported that 7 days of BCAA ‘loading’ in resistance-trained participants attenuated increases in serum creatine kinase (a muscle damage marker) and perceived soreness following one bout of drop-jump induced muscle damage. Other research has shown that BCAAs may foster a beneficial hormonal environment as well as blunt the rise in serum creatine kinase levels following intense resistance exercise [ 13 ]. Nosaka et al. [ 14 ] reported that BCAA supplementation in untrained individuals reduced muscle damage and soreness when consumed immediately before and during a 4-d recovery period of an eccentric leg extensor bout. However, opposite findings also exist. For instance, White et al. [ 15 ] reported that carbohydrate/protein supplementation did not have an effect on muscle soreness, performance or serum creatine kinase levels following eccentric quadriceps contractions. Stock et al. [ 16 ] similarly reported that a leucine/carbohydrate beverage provided to subjects prior to and after 6 sets of heavy back squats did not affect serum creatine kinase, serum lactate dehydrogenase, or muscle soreness up to 72 h following exercise. These authors also reported that back squat performance was not improved with leucine/carbohydrate beverage administration 72 h following the initial heavy squat. While there is some evidence to suggest that amino acid supplementation may be beneficial for promoting various facets of post-exercise skeletal muscle recovery (i.e., increasing muscle protein synthesis and reducing muscle protein breakdown), there are also studies finding that BCAAs are not useful in improving markers of muscle damage, soreness and performance during or following acute exercise protocols. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to compare the effects of BCAA and carbohydrate (BCAA-CHO) versus carbohydrate (i.e., sports drink; CHO) supplementation on markers of muscle damage and performance as well as gross immunological markers during and after a 3-day high intensity back squat protocol. Based upon the aforementioned literature, we hypothesized that BCAA-CHO would attenuate performance decrements and/or positively affect muscle damage markers compared to CHO supplementation.

core_effect_and_quantification.activity_context: During and following three consecutive high intensity and high-volume resistance training bouts
core_effect_and_quantification.magnitude_quantification: Increased over the intervention (p = 0.027 main effect of time), with a tendency for increase at T2 relative to T1 (p = 0.055); not differentially altered by BCAA-CHO versus CHO supplementation.

core_effect_and_quantification.activity_context: During and following three consecutive high intensity and high-volume resistance training bouts
core_effect_and_quantification.magnitude_quantification: Increased over the intervention (p < 0.001 main effect of time), with significant increases 24h post-bout 1, 24h post bout 2, and 48h post bout 3 relative to T1 (p <= 0.001); not differentially altered by BCAA-CHO versus CHO supplementation.

core_effect_and_quantification.activity_context: Following three consecutive high intensity and high-volume resistance training bouts with BCAA-CHO vs CHO supplementation
core_effect_and_quantification.direction_of_change: attenuated increases (prevented the rise) with BCAA-CHO supplementation compared to CHO supplementation
core_effect_and_quantification.magnitude_quantification: p = 0.01 (group*time interaction); specifically p = 0.049 (24h post-bout 1 BCAA-CHO vs CHO), p < 0.001 (24h post bout 2 BCAA-CHO vs CHO), and p < 0.001 (48h post bout 3 BCAA-CHO vs CHO).

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Post-exercise branched chain amino acid and carbohydrate (BCAA-CHO) supplementation following high intensity, high-volume resistance training; also encompasses strenuous physical activity and the prevention of exercise-induced monocyte elevation.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: Amino acid ingestion generally enhances post-exercise recovery by increasing skeletal muscle protein synthesis and reducing muscle proteolysis, and potentially reducing post-exercise skeletal muscle inflammation and oxidative stress. Increases in serum myoglobin concentration are a valid marker of muscle damage. Specifically, BCAA-CHO supplementation attenuated increases in monocyte percentages, suggesting an effect on the immune system/inflammation. The ability of BCAAs to prevent this elevation may suggest anti-inflammatory properties, potentially by modulating monocyte differentiation into macrophages or by affecting glutamine synthesis, though the specific molecular mechanism requires further investigation.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: The study compared BCAA-CHO supplementation (two servings containing 3g/d L-leucine, 1g/d L-isoleucine, 2g/d L-valine, 2g non-sugar carbohydrates, 10 kcal, with 3g L-leucine posited as a threshold for muscle protein synthesis) against carbohydrate-only (CHO) supplementation (42g of CHO, 40g sugar, 168 kcal from Powerade). The intervention involved three consecutive high-intensity resistance training bouts (10 sets x 5 repetitions at 80% of 1RM barbell back squat for 3 consecutive days), described as a 'too much of a muscle-damaging stimulus' compared to single-bout protocols.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: BCAA-CHO supplementation specifically attenuated or prevented the rise in monocyte percentages compared to CHO supplementation (at 24h post-bout 1 (p = 0.049), 24h post bout 2 (p < 0.001), and 48h post bout 3 (p < 0.001)), suggesting a specific anti-inflammatory effect for this biomarker. However, it was not specific in mitigating muscle damage or improving performance recovery, as similar decrements were observed in 1RM squat strength and isokinetic peak torque, and serum myoglobin concentrations and perceived muscle soreness increased regardless of supplementation type, indicating no specific benefit of BCAA-CHO over CHO for these markers.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Healthy resistance-trained males (n=30), regularly participating in resistance exercise (>=3 days per week for at least 3 months), and individuals engaged in rigorous resistance training, practitioners, or athletes in free-living environments.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: High-volume resistance training leads to decrements in muscle performance (strength, torque, EMG activity), increases in serum myoglobin and perceived muscle soreness, and decreases in resistance training volume. BCAA-CHO supplementation did not generally mitigate these effects or reduce decrements in lower body strength or improve select markers of muscle damage/soreness compared to CHO supplementation. However, BCAA-CHO supplementation did attenuate or prevent exercise-induced increases in monocyte percentages, which may indicate a modulated inflammatory or stress response to intense exercise, suggesting possible anti-inflammatory effects and a potential benefit in post-training recovery facilitation related to immune responses.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: For most performance, muscle damage, and soreness markers, BCAA-CHO supplementation provided no specific protective benefit or advantage over CHO supplementation under intense and consecutive resistance exercise protocols. However, it demonstrated a potential protective benefit against exercise-induced inflammation by attenuating the training-induced increase in monocyte percentages. There is also diagnostic utility for detecting muscle damage.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: The reliability of BCAA effects on muscle damage, soreness, and performance is context-dependent, with inconsistent findings across studies attributed to variations in exercise protocols (intensity, duration) and supplement timing. While some studies suggest benefits, others (including this one for most markers) find no significant improvement with BCAA compared to control or CHO. Increases in serum myoglobin concentration are considered a valid marker of muscle damage, being more sensitive and less variable than creatine kinase. The study ensured robust statistical analysis by applying Bonferroni corrections for multiple comparisons and Huynh-Feldt correction when sphericity was not met.
recommended_alternatives: skeletal muscle biopsies for analysis of infiltrating inflammatory cells
skeletal muscle biopsies for histological signs of muscle damage
